task_title: Fitness for Flight: Alcohol, Drugs and Fatigue
area: Area I. Pilot Privileges and Currency
objective: By the end of this lesson you can state the 91.17, 91.19 and 61.53 rules as they read today, judge how long to wait after alcohol or a medicine, and use IMSAFE to make an honest go or no-go call on your own fitness.
why: Pilot impairment contributes to many more accidents than aircraft system failures. The rules set a floor, but a hangover, a cold pill or a short night can leave you legal and still unsafe.

prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.15 and 61.16

prereading.what: Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency, for medical certificate holders and driver's license (BasicMed and sport) pilots.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.53

prereading.label: PHAK Ch 17, 17-12 to 17-18

warmup: You finished your last beer at 11 p.m. and your 7 a.m. departure is legal by the clock. What else would you check about yourself before you go?

key_terms.def: Anyone assigned to perform duty in an aircraft during flight time. 91.17 applies to all of them, not just the PIC.
Grams of alcohol per deciliter of blood, or per 210 liters of breath. The limit is below 0.04.
The time between your last drink and acting as a crewmember. The rule says at least 8 hours; the AIM suggests 12 to 24.
After-effects of drinking. PHAK says you are still under the influence of alcohol while you have one.
Cells cannot use the oxygen they get. Alcohol and some drugs cause it.
The time between recommended or prescribed doses of a medicine, such as every 5 to 6 hours.
Short-term tiredness after effort, excitement or lack of sleep. Rest and 8 hours of sound sleep usually cure it.
Long-term fatigue, often from ongoing stress. Rest alone does not fix it; see a physician.
A DUI-type conviction, or a license suspension, revocation or denial for driving impaired. Report it to the FAA within 60 days.
Personal checklist: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion.

body.p: The rule covers anyone who acts or even attempts to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. A crewmember is anyone assigned to perform duty in the aircraft during flight time [[60:4|14 CFR 1.1]]. That includes you as PIC. It also includes a safety pilot, because 91.109(c) requires one in the other control seat during simulated instrument flight [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]].

head: 91.17(a)
No crewmember duty...
What it means
rows: Within 8 hours after drinking any alcoholic beverage [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]]
A time limit. One drink restarts the 8-hour clock.
While under the influence of alcohol [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(2)]]
A performance limit. It applies even after 8 hours [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].
While using any drug that affects your faculties in any way contrary to safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]]
Covers prescription, over-the-counter and illegal drugs.
With an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater in blood or breath [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(4)]]
A quantity limit: grams per deciliter of blood or per 210 liters of breath.

body.p: All four apply at once. If your blood alcohol is still 0.04 or more after 8 hours, you cannot fly until it falls below that. If it is well below 0.04, you still cannot fly sooner than 8 hours after drinking [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

callout.text: Common mistake: thinking "8 hours bottle to throttle" is the whole rule. It is only one of four limits. The PHAK adds that it is a good idea to be more conservative than the regulations [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

Common mistake: using the driving limit. Figure 17-8 notes that most states use 0.08 or 0.10 for driving [[1:437|PHAK Figure 17-8]]. For flying the number is 0.04, half or less of that [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(4)]].

check.q: Your safety pilot had a beer 5 hours ago and says she feels fine. Can she serve as your safety pilot today?
check.a: No. She would be a crewmember within 8 hours after drinking [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]] [[60:4|14 CFR 1.1]].

chunks.title: How alcohol hits a pilot, and why 8 hours may not be enough

body.p: Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant that acts much like a general anesthetic [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]]. As little as one ounce of liquor, one bottle of beer or four ounces of wine can impair flying skills [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]]. Even one drink can impair vision and hearing [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

bullets: Your blood absorbs about 80 to 90 percent of a drink's alcohol within 30 minutes on an empty stomach [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
Your body needs about 3 hours to clear the alcohol in one beer or one mixed drink [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]]. Nothing speeds it up or cures a hangover [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]].
Considerable alcohol can stay in your body for over 16 hours [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

Altitude multiplies the effect: two drinks at altitude may act like three or four [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]]. One ounce of alcohol can equal about 2,000 ft of extra physiological altitude [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Alcohol can cause inner-ear disturbance and spatial disorientation for up to 48 hours [[1:439|PHAK Figure 17-9]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "I'm hung over, but I'm past 8 hours, so I'm legal." While you have a hangover you are still under the influence of alcohol [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]], and 91.17(a)(2) bans that [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(2)]].

AIM: a pilot may still be under the influence 8 hours after a moderate amount of alcohol. An excellent rule is 12 to 24 hours between bottle and throttle, depending on how much you drank [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]].

check.q: About how long does your body need to clear the alcohol from one beer?

chunks.title: Testing, refusals, passengers and your driving record

body.p: **Police tests.** A crewmember must submit to a blood or breath alcohol test when a law enforcement officer asks, if state or local law authorizes the officer to test, and the officer is investigating a suspected violation of a state or local law covering the same or similar conduct as 91.17(a)(1), (2) or (4) [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(c)(1)]].

**FAA requests.** If the FAA has a reasonable basis to believe you broke the alcohol rules, you must give it the results of each alcohol test taken within 4 hours after you acted or attempted to act as a crewmember, or authorize their release [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(c)(2)]]. The same applies to drug test results under 91.17(a)(3) [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(d)]]. The FAA may use those results to judge your qualifications and as evidence [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(e)]].

head: If you...
It is grounds for
rows: Denial of an application for up to 1 year after the act, or suspension or revocation of any certificate or rating [[60:201|14 CFR 61.15(b)]] [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(b)(1)-(2)]]
Refuse a police alcohol test or refuse to release results to the FAA
Denial for up to 1 year after the refusal, or suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.16]] [[60:203|14 CFR 61.16(a)-(b)]]
Have two motor vehicle actions within 3 years (separate incidents)
Denial for up to 1 year after the last one, or suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(d)]]
Fail to report a motor vehicle action to the FAA within 60 days
Denial for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)-(f)]]

body.p: A motor vehicle action is a conviction for driving impaired or under the influence of alcohol or a drug, or a driver's license suspension, revocation or denial for that reason [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(c)]]. The written report goes to the FAA Civil Aviation Security Division (AMC-700) in Oklahoma City [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]].

callout.text: Passengers: except in an emergency, no pilot may allow a person who appears intoxicated, or shows by manner or physical signs that they are under the influence of drugs, to be carried. A medical patient under proper care is the exception [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(b)]].

check.q: The FAA has reason to believe you flew within 8 hours of drinking. Which test results can it ask you to hand over?
check.a: The results of each alcohol test taken within 4 hours after you acted or attempted to act as a crewmember [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(c)(2)]].

body.p: The regulations contain no specific list of medicines. Two rules matter most [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]:

bullets: **91.17(a)(3):** no crewmember duty while using any drug that affects your faculties in any way contrary to safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]].

**61.53(a):** if you hold a medical certificate, you may not act as PIC or as a required pilot crewmember while you know or have reason to know of a condition that would make you unable to meet the standards for that medical, or while taking medication or treatment that makes you unable to meet them [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]].

body.p: **Driver's license pilots.** For 61.23(c) operations, such as BasicMed under 61.113(i), a pilot who holds a U.S. driver's license uses the 61.53(b) test: no flying while you know or have reason to know of any condition that would make you unable to operate the aircraft safely [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(v)]] [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(b)-(c)]]. BasicMed pilots sign a statement saying exactly that [[60:405|14 CFR 68.3(b)(5)]].

**Carrying drugs.** No person may operate a civil aircraft in the United States knowing that narcotic drugs, marihuana, or depressant or stimulant drugs or substances are on board, unless the carriage is authorized by a federal or state statute or agency [[60:438|14 CFR 91.19]]. A conviction under any drug statute is grounds for denial for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation [[60:201|14 CFR 61.15(a)]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "Marijuana is legal in my state, so it's fine off duty." The FAA has stated: "Marijuana is an illicit drug per federal law and its use by airmen is prohibited" [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]]. Illicit drugs significantly raise accident risk [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

Changed: AIM 8-1-1a(1) still says all pilots except glider and balloon pilots must hold a medical certificate [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1a]]. Today 61.23(c) also allows a U.S. driver's license for sport pilots and BasicMed flights [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)]]. Either way, 61.53 grounds you when you are not fit [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53]].

check.q: You fly under BasicMed. What 61.53 standard grounds you?
check.a: Knowing or having reason to know of any medical condition that would make you unable to operate the aircraft safely [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(b)-(c)]] [[60:405|14 CFR 68.3(b)(5)]].

chunks.title: Common medicines and what they do to you

body.p: Virtually every medicine can cause side effects in some people. Herbal supplements, energy boosters and "natural" products can too [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. A drug with no side effects on the ground can cause serious problems even at normal GA altitudes. Fatigue, stress, dehydration, poor nutrition and taking several drugs at once make side effects worse [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

head: Medicine
What the FAA sources say
rows: Antihistamines and decongestants (cold and allergy pills)
Can cause drowsiness and cognitive deficits. Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) stays in your system a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].
Tranquilizers, sedatives, strong pain relievers, cough suppressants
Primary effects may impair judgment, memory, alertness, coordination, vision and math [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1c]].
Blood pressure drugs, muscle relaxants, diarrhea and motion sickness drugs
Side effects may impair the same functions [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1c]].
Aspirin, acetaminophen, ibuprofen at the correct dose
Few side effects; flying usually not restricted [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].
Prescription painkillers (for example oxycodone, codeine)
Flying is almost always precluded: confusion, dizziness, headaches, nausea, vision problems [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].
Some antibiotics
Can cause balance problems, hearing loss, nausea. The infection itself may ground you [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

bullets: Any medicine that depresses the nervous system, such as a sedative, tranquilizer or antihistamine, makes you much more susceptible to hypoxia [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1c]].
The condition you are treating may itself be disqualifying, apart from the medicine [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].
Unless a physician prescribes it, don't take more than one drug at a time, and never mix drugs with alcohol [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
After dental work, the local anesthetic usually wears off soon; the procedure and the pain afterward may limit you more [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

check.q: Why is a diphenhydramine sleep aid at bedtime a problem for a morning flight?
check.a: It causes drowsiness and has a prolonged half-life, so it stays in your system and its side effects last longer [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

chunks.title: How long to wait after a medicine

body.p: The safest rule is not to fly as a crewmember while taking any medication unless the FAA has approved it. If in doubt about a medicine's effects, ask an aviation medical examiner (AME) before flying [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]] [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1c]].

head: Situation
PHAK guidance
rows: Any new medicine, OTC or prescription
Wait at least 48 hours after the first dose to make sure you have no side effects that make flying unsafe [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]
A medicine with possible sedating or dizzy side effects
Wait at least five maximal dosing intervals after the last dose. The PHAK example: an interval of 5 to 6 hours means waiting 30 hours (5 x 6) [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]
Unnecessary or elective medicines
Don't take them before flying [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]

body.p: Use the longest interval on the label. Everyone metabolizes medicines differently, so even the dosing interval does not remove all risk; five intervals is a reasonable rule of thumb [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

callout.text: New pill: 48 hours. Drowsy pill: 5 x the longest dosing interval. Doubt: ask an AME [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

check.q: A sedating allergy pill says one dose every 8 to 12 hours. How long after your last dose should you wait?

chunks.title: Fatigue: acute, chronic, skill fatigue and sleep apnea

body.p: Fatigue is one of the most treacherous hazards to flight safety, because you may not notice it until you make serious errors [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1e]]. It degrades attention and concentration, coordination and the ability to communicate, and so your decisions [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

head: Type
What it is
Fix
rows: Acute
Short-term tiredness after hard effort, excitement or lack of sleep [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]
Rest and 8 hours of sound sleep ordinarily cure it [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]
Skill fatigue (a kind of acute fatigue)
Timing of each part of a task is slightly off, and attention narrows to the center of vision [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]
Rest before you fly
Chronic
Not enough recovery between bouts of acute fatigue; judgment fails and you take unwarranted risks [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1e]]
A prolonged period of rest [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1e]]; see a physician [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]

body.p: If you have acute fatigue, stay on the ground. If fatigue shows up in the flight deck, no amount of training or experience can overcome it. Avoid flying without a full night's rest, after excessive work hours, or after an exhausting or stressful day [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

**Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)** interrupts restorative sleep. Signs: snoring, daytime sleepiness, breathing pauses in sleep, memory and concentration problems. OSA is easily treated, and most treatments are acceptable for medical certification once shown to work [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1e(4)]].

callout.text: Dehydration also starts as fatigue. Coffee, tea, alcohol and caffeinated sodas are diuretics. Drink water on long flights whether or not you are thirsty [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]] [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

check.q: Fatigue starts to creep in on final after a long day. Can experience make up for it?
check.a: No. No amount of training or experience overcomes fatigue in the flight deck; rest is the only prevention [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

body.p: **Illness.** Even a minor illness can produce fever and distracting symptoms that impair judgment, memory, alertness and calculation. A medicine may control the symptoms but hurt your performance. The safest rule is not to fly with any illness; if that seems too strict, ask an AME [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1b]].

**Stress** is the body's response to physical and psychological demands [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Acute stress is short term, and a healthy person usually copes. Chronic stress, from money, relationship or work problems, can exceed your ability to cope, and performance falls off fast. A pilot at that level is not safe and should not use airman privileges [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

bullets: The regulations don't list stress as a grounding condition, so you must judge it yourself [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].
Most pilots don't leave stress on the ground. When difficulties pile up, consider delaying the flight until they are resolved [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1f]].
Stress and fatigue together are an extremely hazardous combination [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1f]].

body.p: **Emotion.** A serious argument, a death in the family, divorce, job loss or a financial blow can leave you unable to fly safely. Anger, depression and anxiety cut alertness and can lead to risk taking. Don't fly until you have recovered [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1g]] [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1g]].

check.q: You had a heated argument with your business partner an hour before a planned flight. What does the AIM say?
check.a: Emotionally upsetting events can make you unable to fly safely; don't fly until you have satisfactorily recovered [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1g]] [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1g]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: the IMSAFE check

body.p: Pilot impairment contributes to many more accidents than aircraft system failures, so check yourself before every flight just as you check the airplane [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1h]].

bullets: 1. **The day before.** Set your alcohol cutoff (12 to 24 hours [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]]), plan for a full night's sleep [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]], and don't start a new medicine within 48 hours of the flight [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
2. **Illness:** any symptoms, even mild ones? Even mild symptoms can be a pilot hazard [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].
3. **Medication:** anything taken, prescription or OTC, within five maximal dosing intervals [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]?
4. **Stress:** work, money, health or family pressure [[30:24|RMH Figure 3-3]]?
5. **Alcohol:** within 8 hours? Within 24 hours? Any after-effects [[30:24|RMH Figure 3-3]] [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]?
6. **Fatigue** and **Emotion:** tired or not adequately rested? Emotionally upset [[30:24|RMH Figure 3-3]]?
7. **Decide.** Any yes is a pilot hazard. Mitigate it, raise your personal minimums, or don't go. Options include waiting, delaying, cancelling or driving [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

body.p: A numerical flight risk assessment tool (FRAT) puts numbers on the same hazards. You add the scores, and the total falls in a low-risk, exercise-caution or danger range [[30:28|RMH 3-10]].

callout.text: Some publications use the E in IMSAFE for Eating. Food and water matter on any long flight, so check both [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

check.q: On Figure 3-6 you slept under 8 hours, feel a bit off, expect 3 miles and 1,500 ft ceilings at the destination, fly at night, are in no hurry, your day is going great, and you score 0 on every other planning item. What is your total and range?

chunks.title: Risk: legal, but not fit to fly

body.p: Safe pilots know the difference between what is legal under the regulations and what is smart or safe [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. The 91.17 limits are a floor. Hangover effects can stay a pilot hazard for longer than 8 hours [[30:23|RMH 3-5]], and a medicine taken yesterday can still be in your system [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

**You are a poor judge of yourself.** Ask a pilot who has flown 16 hours whether they are too tired to continue, and the answer may be "no." Goal-oriented pilots tend to deny their limits [[1:45|PHAK 2-6]]. A stressed or fatigued pilot may find it hard or impossible to focus [[30:45|RMH 6-2]], and fatigue keeps pilots from taking extra steps to check what they think they see [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

head: Hazard
Hidden risk
rows: Hangover
Still under the influence; motor and mental impairment remain [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]]
Last night's drinks
Inner-ear disturbance and spatial disorientation up to 48 hours [[1:439|PHAK Figure 17-9]]
Antihistamine, sedative, alcohol
Much more susceptible to hypoxia [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a(4)]]
Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue
More likely to suffer spatial disorientation [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]

body.p: When you face illness, medication, stress or fatigue, the RMH example adds at least 500 ft to your ceiling minimum [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]]. Make these adjustments ahead of time, not to complete a specific flight under pressure [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "I passed IMSAFE in my head, so I'm fine." Be honest. In the RMH case study the pilot names alcohol and lack of sleep as hazards, then mitigates them: no alcohol, an early dinner, early to bed and more water [[30:36|RMH 4-3]] [[30:41|RMH 5-3]].

check.q: Your personal ceiling minimum is 1,000 ft. You slept badly and have a mild cold. Using the RMH example, what is your adjusted minimum?
check.a: At least 1,500 ft (add at least 500 ft for illness or fatigue) [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]], and the AIM's safest rule is not to fly with any illness [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1b]].

bullets: Counting 8 hours and ignoring the hangover rule [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(2)]] [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
Using the 0.08 driving limit instead of 0.04 [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(4)]].
Thinking 91.17 applies only to the PIC; it applies to every crewmember [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]].
Taking a new cold or allergy medicine the night before a flight instead of 48 hours ahead [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
Treating OTC as harmless; antihistamines and decongestants cause drowsiness [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].
Believing coffee or sleep cures chronic fatigue [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].
Forgetting to report a DUI-type motor vehicle action within 60 days [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]].
Lowering personal minimums to finish today's trip [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

check.q: Which of these errors applies to a pilot who says, "OTC means it's safe"?
check.a: Treating OTC drugs as harmless. Antihistamines and decongestants can cause drowsiness and cognitive deficits [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

f1.caption: Figure 17-8. Impairment scale with alcohol use.
f1.alt: Blue table. Top part lists typical servings and pure alcohol content: table wine 4 oz (.48), light beer 12 oz (.48), aperitif liquor 1.5 oz (.38), champagne 4 oz (.48), vodka 1 oz (.50), whiskey 1.25 oz (.50). Lower part lists blood alcohol ranges from 0.01-0.05% (appears normal) up to 0.35-0.50% (unconsciousness, possible death), with effects for each range. Footnote: legal limit for driving in most states is 0.08 or 0.10%.

f2.caption: Figure 17-9. Adverse affects of various drugs.
f2.alt: Table with columns substance, generic or brand name, treatment for, and possible side effects, for alcohol, nicotine, amphetamines, caffeine, antacids, antihistamines and aspirin. Alcohol row includes inner-ear disturbance and spatial disorientation up to 48 hours; antihistamine row lists drowsiness and dizziness; aspirin row lists hypoxia and hyperventilation.

f3.caption: Figure 3-3. IMSAFE checklist.
f3.alt: Notepad page titled I'M SAFE CHECKLIST with a pencil. Illness: do I have any symptoms? Medication: have I been taking prescription or over-the-counter drugs? Stress: am I under psychological pressure from the job, worried about money, health or family? Alcohol: have I been drinking within 8 hours, within 24 hours? Fatigue: am I tired and not adequately rested? Emotion: am I emotionally upset?

f4.caption: Figure 2-9. Examples of additional safety margins from baseline personal minimums.
f4.alt: Four colored rows. Pilot (yellow): illness, medication, stress or fatigue, or lack of currency: add at least 500 feet to ceiling. Aircraft (blue): unfamiliar airplane or avionics: add at least 1/2 mile to visibility. Environment (green): unfamiliar airports, airspace or terrain: add at least 500 feet to runway length. External pressures (red): must-meet deadlines or passenger pressure: subtract at least 5 knots from winds.

f5.caption: Figure 3-6. Example of a numerical FRAT.
f5.alt: Risk assessment form with scored items: sleep (did not sleep well or less than 8 hours 2, slept well 0), how do you feel (cold or ill 4, feel great 0, a bit off 2), weather at termination (1, 3 or 4 for IMC), how is the day going (3 or 0), day 1 or night 3, and planning items. Below, a total score scale from 0 to 30: not complex flight 0-10, exercise caution 10-20, area of concern 20-30, ending in endangerment.

scenario.title: Legal by the clock after a wedding
scenario.setup: You are an instrument-rated commercial pilot. You promised a friend a 7:00 a.m. flight home in the club's single-engine airplane, about 2 hours, with a forecast 900 ft overcast at the destination. Your personal ceiling minimum is 800 ft. At a wedding the night before you had three glasses of champagne, the last at 10:45 p.m. You got home at 1:00 a.m., took a new cold medicine with diphenhydramine to help you sleep, and slept about 5 hours. You wake with a headache and a stuffy nose.

questions.q: Does the 8-hour rule allow a 7:00 a.m. departure?
questions.a: By the clock only: 10:45 p.m. + 8 hours = 6:45 a.m. [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]]. But a hangover means you are still under the influence [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]], which 91.17(a)(2) bans, and the AIM suggests 12 to 24 hours [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]].

It is a new medicine, so wait at least 48 hours after the first dose. Diphenhydramine causes drowsiness and stays in the system a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]] [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. Flying while a drug affects your faculties breaks 91.17(a)(3) [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]].

questions.q: Your stuffy nose is mild. Does that matter?
questions.a: Yes. Even a minor illness can impair judgment and alertness; the safest rule is not to fly with any illness [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1b]]. Alcohol, medication, illness and fatigue also raise the chance of spatial disorientation in the clouds [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

questions.q: Apply the RMH personal-minimums adjustment. Is the 900 ft forecast acceptable?
questions.a: No. With illness, medication or fatigue, add at least 500 ft: 800 + 500 = 1,300 ft, above the 900 ft forecast [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]].

questions.q: Your friend says you look fine and will be disappointed. What do you do?
questions.a: Hold the no-go. Pilots tend to deny their own limits [[1:45|PHAK 2-6]]. Offer to delay, cancel or drive [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. A written set of personal minimums makes the tough call easier to explain [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

skills.do: Given a pilot's last 24 to 48 hours (drinks, medicines, sleep, illness, stress, upsetting events) and a planned flight, run IMSAFE, name the rules that apply (91.17, 91.19, 61.53), and make and explain a go, delay or no-go decision at a flight review, IPC or WINGS session.
skills.practice: Before every flight for a month, run Figure 3-3 out loud and write down any yes [[30:24|RMH Figure 3-3]]. Score one trip on a numerical FRAT [[30:28|RMH 3-10]], and write baseline personal minimums with the illness, medication, stress and fatigue add-ons [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Have your instructor give you made-up "last 24 hours" cases to judge against 91.17 and the PHAK medication waits [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]] [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four limits in 14 CFR 91.17(a)?
options: Within 8 hours after drinking any alcoholic beverage
While under the influence of alcohol
An alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater
Within 12 hours after drinking more than two drinks
quiz.why: 91.17(a) sets 8 hours, under the influence, drugs affecting faculties, and 0.04 [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. 12 to 24 hours is AIM advice, not a rule [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]].

quiz.q: What does the PHAK say about a pilot with a hangover?
options: Legal once 8 hours have passed
Fine if a breath test reads below 0.04
Still under the influence of alcohol
Impaired only above 10,000 ft
quiz.why: While experiencing a hangover, a pilot is still under the influence; motor and mental impairment remain [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

quiz.q: At altitude, two drinks may have the effect of about how many?
options: Three or four
Five or six
One
Two
quiz.why: Altitude multiplies alcohol's effect: two drinks may act like three or four [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

quiz.q: You refuse a breath test that a police officer properly requests under 91.17(c). What can happen?
options: Nothing, it is a state matter only
Denial of applications for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation
An automatic 30-day suspension only
A required new practical test
quiz.why: A refusal is grounds for denial for up to 1 year or suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.16]] [[60:203|14 CFR 61.16(a)-(b)]].

quiz.q: Under 91.19, when may you operate a civil aircraft knowing that marihuana is on board?
options: When it is legal in both departure and destination states
When the amount is for personal use
Only when a federal or state statute or agency authorizes the carriage
Whenever you are not the one using it
quiz.why: The ban does not apply only to carriage authorized by or under a federal or state statute or agency [[60:438|14 CFR 91.19]].

quiz.q: Why is diphenhydramine (Benadryl) singled out in the PHAK?
options: It is a stimulant that hides fatigue
It raises blood pressure at altitude
It causes drowsiness and has a prolonged half-life
It reacts with avgas fumes
quiz.why: It is known to cause drowsiness and stays in the system for an extended time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

quiz.q: You start a new prescription. How long does the PHAK say to wait after the first dose before flying?
options: 8 hours
At least 48 hours
24 hours
Five days
quiz.why: Wait at least 48 hours after the first dose of any new OTC or prescription medicine [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

options: One full night of sleep
A prolonged period of rest, and usually a physician
A good meal
Caffeine before the flight
quiz.why: Recovery takes a prolonged period of rest [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1e]]; chronic fatigue isn't relieved by diet and sleep and usually needs a physician [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

quiz.q: Which hazard does the RMH say some publications fold into the S of IMSAFE, using the E for Eating?
options: Stress
Supplements
Sleep
Emotion
quiz.why: Some publications combine Emotion with Stress and use the E for Eating [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

quiz.q: Facing illness, medication, stress or fatigue, how much does the RMH example add to your ceiling minimum?
options: At least 500 ft
At least 1,000 ft
At least 200 ft
Nothing if you are current
quiz.why: Figure 2-9 adds at least 500 ft to the ceiling for those pilot factors [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]].

takeaways: 91.17(a) has four limits at once: 8 hours, not under the influence, no impairing drugs, below 0.04.
A hangover is still "under the influence." The AIM suggests 12 to 24 hours, not 8.
Submit to a proper police test, hand over test results the FAA asks for, and report a motor vehicle action within 60 days.
New medicine: wait 48 hours. Drowsy medicine: wait five of the longest dosing intervals. In doubt, ask an AME.
61.53 grounds you when you know or should know you are not fit, medical or BasicMed.
Run IMSAFE honestly before every flight. Any yes means mitigate, raise your minimums, or stay on the ground.
cfi_notes: Pilots remember "8 hours bottle to throttle" and forget the rest of 91.17(a). Ask them to list all four limits and explain the hangover line on PHAK 17-15.
PHAK 17-15 says blood alcohol must be "less than .04 percent"; the rule bans 0.04 "or greater" in blood or breath. Same limit, but point out that a breath test counts too.

AIM 8-1-1a(1) still says all pilots except glider and balloon pilots need a medical certificate. Teach 61.23(c): sport pilots and BasicMed flights may use a U.S. driver's license, and those pilots use the 61.53(b) "unable to operate safely" test.

The 48-hour first-dose wait and the five-maximal-dosing-interval rule are PHAK guidance, not regulation. Many experienced pilots have never heard them; make students work an example with a real label's interval.
Figure 17-9 uses many old brand names. Teach the drug classes (antihistamine, analgesic, stimulant, depressant) so pilots can read any label.
A safety pilot is a crewmember too. Examiners and reviewers like the "safety pilot had a beer at lunch" question.
For R1, push past the legal answer: have the pilot set written alcohol, sleep and medication cutoffs before the day of the flight, as RMH 2-5 advises for personal minimums.
gaps: The FAA's Do Not Issue / Do Not Fly medication list and the AME Guide are named in AC 68-1A but are not in the sources, so the lesson gives no drug-by-drug approvals.
The FAA OTC medication web page that RMH 3-5 links to is not in the sources.
State laws on when police may test a pilot (91.17(c)(1)) vary and are not covered.
Part 120 drug and alcohol testing programs for Part 121 and 135 operators are not in the sources and are outside this Part 91 lesson.
Sleep science details (circadian rhythm, sleep debt, napping) and airline duty-time rules are not covered by the GA handbooks used here.

activities.title: Bottle to throttle
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You plan to take off at 0630. Under 91.17(a)(1), what is the latest clock time you may finish a drink? Type it as hhmm, 24-hour.
items.why: 0630 minus 8 hours = 2230 the night before [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]].

items.q: Your last drink was at 2000 and you plan to leave at 0600. How many more hours would you need to wait to meet the short end of the AIM's 12-to-24-hour advice?
Using Figure 17-8, how many ounces of pure alcohol are in two 4-ounce glasses of table wine?
items.why: Each 4-oz glass has .48 oz, so 2 x .48 = 0.96 oz [[1:437|PHAK Figure 17-8]]. As little as one ounce can impair reflexes [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

items.q: You fly at 6,000 ft after drinking one ounce of alcohol. Using the PHAK research figure, about what physiological altitude does your brain feel?
items.why: One ounce of alcohol can equal an extra 2,000 ft of physiological altitude: 6,000 + 2,000 = 8,000 ft [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

activities.title: Which rule says that?
activities.intro: Tap a rule, then the requirement it sets.

pairs.r: Limits on acting as a crewmember after alcohol or drugs
No carrying an intoxicated person, except in an emergency
Submit to a proper police blood or breath test
Give the FAA alcohol test results from within 4 hours
Refusing a test is grounds for denial, suspension or revocation
Report a motor vehicle action within 60 days

activities.title: Fly or stay down?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Marijuana, in a state where it is legal

activities.title: How long to wait?
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A sedating cold pill says one dose every 6 to 8 hours. How many hours after your last dose should you wait to fly?
items.why: Five maximal dosing intervals: 5 x 8 = 40 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

items.q: You took the first dose of a new prescription Thursday at 2000 and want to fly Saturday at 0800. How many hours short of the 48-hour wait are you?
items.why: Thursday 2000 to Saturday 0800 is 36 hours. 48 - 36 = 12 hours short [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

items.q: Your last dose of an antihistamine (every 8 hours at most) was Friday at 2200. Your flight is Saturday at 1000. How many more hours must you wait?
items.why: 5 x 8 = 40 hours after Friday 2200 is Sunday 1400. Saturday 1000 to Sunday 1400 = 28 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

items.q: A sedating medicine is taken once a day (every 24 hours). How many hours after the last dose should you wait?

activities.title: True or false: fatigue, stress and illness
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Rest and 8 hours of sound sleep ordinarily cure acute fatigue.
Chronic fatigue usually clears up with a good diet and one full night's sleep.
cards.why: False. It is not relieved by diet and sleep and usually needs a physician [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

cards.s: Skill fatigue can narrow your attention to the center of your vision.
cards.why: True. It disrupts the perceptual field and the timing of tasks [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

cards.s: The regulations list stress as a medical condition that grounds a pilot.
cards.why: False. Stress is not among them; you must judge it yourself [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

cards.s: Coffee and caffeinated sodas help prevent dehydration on a long flight.
cards.why: False. They are diuretics that add to water loss [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

cards.s: Loud snoring and daytime sleepiness are symptoms that call for a sleep apnea evaluation.
cards.why: True. Snoring and excessive daytime sleepiness are OSA symptoms [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1e(4)]].

cards.s: If a minor illness seems too small to ground you, the AIM says to ask an AME.
cards.why: True. The safest rule is not to fly with any illness; if that seems too strict, contact an AME [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1b]].

activities.title: Can I fly Saturday morning?
activities.intro: You are an instrument-rated private pilot with a current third-class medical. On Saturday at 0700 you plan a 2-hour IFR trip in N4471K, a club Cessna 172, taking two friends to a lunch. Your written ceiling minimum is 1,000 ft. On Friday evening you are at a dinner party.

steps.s: Friday 1830. Your host offers wine and the party will run late. What is your plan?
options: Skip alcohol tonight, or stop by 1900 so at least 12 hours pass
Drink until 2300; 0700 is exactly 8 hours later
Drink freely and check a breath tester in the morning
Drink only beer, since it has less alcohol
steps.why: 8 hours is the legal floor [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]]; you may still be under the influence then, so the AIM suggests 12 to 24 hours [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]]. A 12-oz light beer has as much alcohol as a glass of wine [[1:437|PHAK Figure 17-8]].

steps.s: 2230. Your allergies flare. In your bag is a diphenhydramine sleep aid you have used before.
options: Take it; it will wear off by 0700
Skip it and judge your symptoms in the morning
Take a half dose
Take it and fly only if you don't feel drowsy
steps.why: Diphenhydramine causes drowsiness and stays in your system a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. A sedating dose needs five maximal dosing intervals before flight [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]], and you are a poor judge of your own impairment [[1:45|PHAK 2-6]].

steps.s: Saturday 0530. You slept about 5 hours, your nose is stuffy, and the destination forecast is 1,200 ft overcast. Run IMSAFE.
options: Go: 1,200 ft is above your 1,000 ft minimum
Go, but fly the approach by hand to stay alert
Go, and take a decongestant before departure
Treat illness and fatigue as hazards: add at least 500 ft, so 1,200 ft is below your 1,500 ft limit
steps.why: Illness and fatigue add at least 500 ft to your ceiling minimum [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]]. The AIM's safest rule is not to fly with any illness [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1b]]. A new pill on departure morning breaks the 48-hour advice [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

steps.s: Your friends say they will miss the lunch and that you look fine. What now?
options: Go to keep your promise
Delay to the afternoon without rechecking anything
Stay a no-go: offer to drive or reschedule
Lower your minimums just for today
steps.why: Don't adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Driving, delaying or cancelling are all ways to cut the risk [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

steps.s: Sunday 0700. You slept 8 hours, have no symptoms, took no medicine and drank nothing since Friday. Weather is 3,000 ft and 10 miles.
options: Fly, after a quick IMSAFE check comes up clear
Stay down another day to be safe
Fly, but only with an instructor aboard
Get an AME's approval first
steps.why: Sound sleep cures acute fatigue [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]], and an IMSAFE check with every answer clear means you are fit [[30:24|RMH Figure 3-3]].

final_quiz.q: Nine hours after your last drink, a breath test reads 0.045. May you act as PIC?
options: Yes, 8 hours have passed
Yes, if the flight is under 1 hour
Yes, breath tests don't count
No, not until it falls below 0.04
final_quiz.why: 0.04 or greater in blood or breath grounds you even after 8 hours [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(4)]] [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

final_quiz.q: Six hours after one beer, a breath test reads 0.00. May you fly now?
options: Yes, the reading is zero
Yes, one beer takes only 3 hours to clear
No, 8 hours must pass after any alcoholic drink
Yes, if you feel normal
final_quiz.why: The 8-hour limit applies regardless of the reading [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]] [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

final_quiz.q: A passenger arrives obviously drunk for a routine sightseeing flight. What does 91.17(b) require?
options: Carry them if they are belted in
Carry them only if a second pilot is aboard
Carry them if they sit in the back
Don't carry them, except in an emergency
final_quiz.why: Except in an emergency, a pilot may not allow a person who appears intoxicated to be carried [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(b)]].

final_quiz.q: You were convicted of DUI 20 days ago. What do you owe the FAA?
options: A new flight review
Nothing until your next medical
A phone call within 10 days
A written report within 60 days of the conviction
final_quiz.why: Report each motor vehicle action in writing to the FAA (AMC-700) within 60 days [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]].

final_quiz.q: You have two separate DUI-related license suspensions 2 years apart. What do they mean for your certificate?
options: Nothing, because they are driving matters
They are grounds for denial of applications for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation
Automatic loss of your medical
A required retest of all ratings
final_quiz.why: A motor vehicle action within 3 years of a previous one (separate incidents) is grounds for denial, suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(d)]].

final_quiz.q: You hold a third-class medical and were just diagnosed with a condition you know is disqualifying. Your medical is still unexpired. May you fly as PIC?
options: No, 61.53(a) prohibits it
Yes, under VFR only
Yes, until the medical expires
Yes, if a passenger is a pilot
final_quiz.why: You may not act as PIC while you know of a condition that makes you unable to meet the medical standards [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]].

final_quiz.q: The FAA has a reasonable basis to believe you flew after drinking. A hospital drew your blood 3 hours after you landed. On FAA request, what must you do?
options: Release it only if police also ask
Nothing; medical records are private
Furnish the result or authorize its release
Release it only if the test was within 1 hour
final_quiz.why: You must furnish or authorize release of each alcohol test taken within 4 hours after acting as a crewmember [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(c)(2)]]. Refusing is grounds for denial, suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.16]].

final_quiz.q: A nasal allergy pill is taken every 12 hours. Under the PHAK rule of thumb, how long after the last dose should you wait to fly if it can make you drowsy?
options: 60 hours
24 hours
48 hours
12 hours
final_quiz.why: Five maximal dosing intervals: 5 x 12 = 60 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

final_quiz.q: You had a filling with local anesthetic this morning and feel fine by afternoon. What does the PHAK say?
options: Local anesthetics always ground you for 48 hours
The anesthetic usually wears off soon; the procedure and pain may limit you more
You need an AME's written OK first
Fly only below 5,000 ft
final_quiz.why: Most local anesthetics wear off quickly; the procedure and pain afterward may limit flying more [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

final_quiz.q: On the Figure 3-6 FRAT you slept well, feel great, expect IMC at the destination, fly by day, rushed to get off the ground, and score 0 on every other item. What is your total?
You plan a 12,000 ft cruise after a night of moderate drinking that ended 10 hours ago. What makes this extra risky?
options: Nothing, since you are past 8 hours
Only fuel burn changes at altitude
Alcohol improves night vision at altitude
Alcohol makes you more susceptible to hypoxia, and altitude multiplies its effect
final_quiz.why: Alcohol increases susceptibility to hypoxia [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]], and altitude multiplies its effect on the brain [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot who has flown 16 hours is asked if they are too tired to continue. What does the PHAK say they will likely answer?
options: No, goal-oriented pilots tend to deny their limits
Yes, pilots are honest about fatigue
They will ask for a FRAT
They cannot answer
final_quiz.why: The answer may be "no"; pilots tend to deny personal limitations [[1:45|PHAK 2-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your father died two days ago. You feel calm and want to fly to clear your head. What does the AIM advise?
options: Don't fly until you have satisfactorily recovered
Fly only with a passenger
Fly only in VFR conditions
Fly; it helps you relax
final_quiz.why: After an emotionally upsetting event such as a death in the family, don't fly until satisfactorily recovered [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1g]] [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1g]].

final_quiz.q: Under BasicMed you develop dizzy spells. Which statement is right?
options: You may fly until your next physician exam
You may not act as PIC while you know of a condition that makes you unable to operate safely
BasicMed pilots are exempt from 61.53
You may fly if you take a passenger who is a pilot
final_quiz.why: Driver's license operations under 61.23(c) use the 61.53(b) test [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(b)-(c)]], which BasicMed pilots certify they understand [[60:405|14 CFR 68.3(b)(5)]].
